title: Databases, abstraction and the ER model
subtitle: Why files were not enough, how a database hides storage details, and how to draw the world before building tables.

sections.title: Why a DBMS
sections.body: Storing data in separate files per application leads to redundancy, inconsistency (two copies disagree), no sharing or concurrent safety, and code tied to file formats. A DBMS keeps data in one place and provides a query language, integrity rules, concurrent access, security and recovery after failure. Applications: banking, airline reservation, universities, web sites.

questions.prompt: Which problem of file-based storage does a DBMS mainly solve?

choices.text: Redundant, inconsistent data scattered over application-specific files.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: One shared, controlled copy replaces many.

sections.title: Three levels of abstraction
sections.body: The physical level describes how records are stored (files, indexes); the logical level describes what data exists and their relationships (tables); the view level shows each user only the part they need. Physical data independence: change the storage layout without changing the logical schema. Logical data independence: change the schema without rewriting every view or application. A schema is the design; an instance is the data at this moment.

questions.prompt: Adding an index without changing any query is an example of…

figures.caption: Figure 1.2.1 — three-level architecture
figures.note: Each level hides the one below.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: down
[View level: what each user sees] as v #blue
[Logical level: tables and relationships] as l #mint
[Physical level: files, indexes, blocks] as p #amber
v -> l : mapped by the DBMS
l -> p : mapped by the DBMS");

sections.title: The entity–relationship model
sections.body: An entity is a distinguishable thing (Student, Course); an entity set is a collection of them. Attributes describe entities; a key attribute uniquely identifies one (studentID); composite, multivalued and derived attributes exist. A relationship associates entities (Student enrols in Course) with a cardinality: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A weak entity has no key of its own and depends on an owner (Dependent of Employee).

questions.prompt: Students enrol in many courses; each course has many students. This relationship is…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Both sides can have many partners.

figures.caption: Figure 2.1.1 — Student – Enrolment – Course
figures.note: A many-to-many relationship becomes a third box with two one-to-many links.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
{Student | + id : key ; + name} as s
{Course | + code : key ; + title} as c
{Enrolment | + grade} as e
s -> e : 1 .. many
e -> c : many .. 1");

sections.title: Specialisation, generalisation, aggregation
sections.body: Specialisation splits an entity set into subclasses (Employee → Teacher, Clerk) which inherit attributes; generalisation is the same idea seen bottom-up. Aggregation treats a relationship as an entity so it can take part in another relationship. Constraints: disjoint vs overlapping, total vs partial participation.

figures.caption: Figure 2.2.1 — specialisation
figures.script:
diagram("direction: down
{Person | + id ; + name} as p
{Student | + roll} as s
{Teacher | + salary} as t
s -> p : is a
t -> p : is a");

sections.title: From ER to tables
sections.body: Each strong entity becomes a table (key = primary key). A one-to-many relationship puts the “one” side’s key into the “many” table as a foreign key. A many-to-many relationship becomes its own table whose primary key is the pair of foreign keys, plus the relationship’s attributes. A weak entity’s table includes the owner’s key in its key.

worked.why: Student(id, name), Course(code, title) with a many-to-many “enrols with grade”.
Tables: Student(id, name), Course(code, title), Enrolment(id → Student, code → Course, grade), primary key (id, code).

problems.prompt: A Department has many Employees; each Employee works in exactly one Department. Give the tables.
problems.answer: Department(deptNo, name); Employee(empNo, name, deptNo FK → Department). The foreign key sits on the “many” side.

sections.title: Keys
sections.body: A superkey is any set of attributes that identifies a row; a candidate key is a minimal superkey; the primary key is the candidate chosen; a foreign key references another table’s key. Entity integrity: a primary key is never null. Referential integrity: a foreign key matches an existing key or is null.

choices.text: A minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies rows.
